Stan is survived by his loving wife Suzanne (Anderson) Barney, daughter Stephanie Barney and her partner
Alyssa Sharpe, sister Marie Barney, brother Michael G. Barney and wife Janice, nephew Michael R. Barney
and his fiancée Jillian Doucette, and several nieces, nephews, cousins and extended family. A son, Patrick M.
Stan was blessed with a circle of lifelong friends, many of whom were at his side at the time of his passing.
In his litetime, Stan was involved in a wide range of activities: working at the family business (Barney's Res-
taurant and Dairy Bar), caring for animals, gardening, woodworking, and serving as captain of the Blue
Knights Football Team (#61!). He was an avid Boston sports fan, and was a Celtics season ticket holder for
many years. An avid gardener, Stan maintained beautiful flower and vegetable gardens. He gave away most of
the produce and flowers he grew, including pumpkins, jars of pickles he made with his mother and sister, and
fresh cut flowers. He loved the outdoors and even built his own lumber mill at his residence. Stan loved fishing
and snowmobiling with his friends. Stan was a life member of the Eastwood Club.
A 1968 graduate of Lunenburg High School, Stan attended Merrimack College and graduated from Fitchburg
State University. He married the former Suzanne Anderson of Great Barrington Massachusetts on October 6,
1973. Devoted to the Town of Lunenburg, Stan served for 38 years on the Lunenburg Police Department,
moving through the ranks to Sargent in 2000 and finally Lieutenant in 2013. He cherished serving the commu-
nity as a police officer along with his son. Stan was also a lifetime member of the Lunenburg Police Relief As-
sociation, serving as its President in 1984. He also served several terms as a Cemetery Commissioner for the
Town of Lunenburg, overseeing the maintenance and care of town cemetery grounds.
Stan was also employed by the law enforcement division of the Massachusetts Society for the Prevention of

Local legislative decisions are made by an open town meeting consisting of all registered voters in
the town. Subject to the legislative decisions made by town meeting, the affairs of the town are gen-
erally administered by an elected five member Select Board and a Town Manager, Local school af-
fairs arc administered by an elected seven member School Committee while local taxes are assessed
by an elected three member Board of Assessors.
Lunenburg is a semi-rural community located in northern Worcester County. Lake Whalom and the for-
mer Whalom Amusement Park delineated the Whalom District from the remainder of Lunenburg. This
district was developed as a housing base for many factory workers working in the mills and factories of
Leominster and Fitchburg. In many ways the characteristics of the Whalom District closely reflect charac-
teristics of these cities more than of the rest of Lunenburg. The Hickory Hills Lake area was developed as
a private community comprised largely of vacation cottages. Shirley Reservoir is a public water body also
developed with mainly vacation cottages that have now been moditied to year-round residences.
Commercial and industrial development is permitted in several areas of town, primarily along the two
major arteries (Routes 2A and 13) and the town's peripheries, due largely to the close proximity of
Leominster's and Fitchburg's sewer and water systems. Although many farms and orchards had slow-
ly developed into single family housing, farming continues on in Lunenburg, In 2013 the Annual
Town Meeting voted to establish an Agricultural Commission to represent, preserve and enhance
farming in the community and to administer the "Right to Farm" bylaw,
The 2015 Lunenburg Town Meeting established the Architectural Preservation District ("District")
bylaw to regulate construction, demolition or renovation of existing "Contributing Property" struc-
tures as defined by the bylaw within an established bounded district. The bylaw was introduced at
Town Meeting along with thẹ Village District Bylaw, which created an overlay zoning district to en-
courage mixed-use commercial and residential development. While the Village District Bylaw en-
courages the economic vitalization of downtown Lunenburg, the Architectural Preservation District
Bylaw ensures that it will not come at the expense of the town's historical character and integrity.

effects of the pandemic and a mid-year tax assessment crisis that affected lakefront property owners occurred that im-

valuation adjustment through the Assessors triggered hundreds of abatement applications to be filed and the effects

The Mission Statement of the Board of Assessors is to accurately determine the value of all Real
and Personal Property within the Town of Lunenburg, as outlined in Massachusetts General Law
Chapter 59. The assessed value in every community in the Commonwealth must reflect fair market
value as of January 1 prior to the start of any given fiscal year.
The Assessors are also responsible for the administration of all property tax data records. It
maintains accurate parcel ownership data based on recorded property transactions at the Worcester
North Registry of Deeds. The Assessors process and administer auto excise as well as personal real
estate tax exemptions for the Senior and Surviving Spouse, Blind, and Disabled Veterans.
The Board of Assessors is elected and consists of three members. Each Assessor must complete a
required DOR Training (Course 101, Assessment Administration: Law, Procedures, and Valuation for
assessing board members). In the Town of Lunenburg, the Assessor's office staff consists of a full
time Principal Assessor and a full time Assessors Clerk.
The last 18 months have been tumultuous for the Board of Assessors.
There has been a 100% turnover of the Board of Assessors' membership. 1 new Member was
elected in May 2023, while 2 new Members were appointed to fill vacant slots until May 2024.
The Principal Assessor resigned and was replaced with an Interim Lead Assessor. After a lengthy
search process, a full time Lead Assessor has been identified and will start late March 2024.
The Town has issued a historic number of Property Tax abatements in FY 2023. We handled a 30
x increase in Abatement applications (440 vs 14). The overwhelming majority of the abatements
were settled in a timely fashion.
FY 2024 is a state-mandated 5-Year Revaluation for the every property in Lunenburg. The Prop-
erty Tax abatement effort led to an unprecedented delay in completing that revaluation and de-
termining the tax rate for FY 2024. This resulted in a delay in distribution of the final FY 2024 tax
bills. Because of the unusual and significant work load, two outside agencies, Vision Government
Solutions, Inc. and Municipal Financial Services (MFS), have been engaged to provide assessment
personnel for the abatement process and DOR filings for the 5-year Revaluation.
The Assessor Operations continue be resource-constrained. Currently, we only have 1 Interim
Lead Assessor, and are temporarily short the Assessor Clerk. In the MFS report on the FY2023
Abatement process, it was recommended that Lunenburg add a part time person to help per-
form the normal Assessor Office work load. This included site inspections, office coverage, data
analytics and records maintenance. Currently, the resource constraint is being partially ad-
dressed by the external contractors previously mentioned.
The Board of Assessors is committed to restoring the trust of Lunenburg tax-payers. We hope to
accomplish this through improving transparency, better out-reach, and enhancing visibility and ac-
We have begun this by scheduling all meetings during evenings (with both PACC coverage and
Zoom access), so everyone can participate more easily. We created a Data Collection Manual for use
during the 5-year Revaluation. We are also putting the finishing touches on a guide for "How to Read
Your Vision Property Card", that will be available in hard-copy and via the internet.
To be more inclusive of Lunenburg's tax-payers, we are planning to create an ad hoc, Citizens' Ad-
visory Committee to help us determine to best way to answer citizens questions, prioritize initiatives,
data analysis and generally hold the Board's collective feet to the fire. The Board of Assessors has de-
veloped a Property Tax orientation for use at the Senior Center to explain the options that are availa-
ble to reduce the tax burden for our Senior Citizens.
We are improving visibility and access by embarking on a redesign of the Website. This will in-
clude the resources mentioned above, as well as Frequently Asked Questions. Other information will
include analytics and explanations provided by the Massachusetts DOR/ Division of Local Services,
Massachusetts Association of Assessing Officers, and UMass among others.

Since the School Committee approved the Strategy for Continuous Improvement in November 2019, we have
worked with intent to achieve our vision, putting the necessary infrastructure to support the well-being and academ-
ic achievement of all students in place. The Strategy is a living document reviewed by the District Leadership
Team each August. In August 2023, the Strategy objectives were consolidated from four original objectives to a
singular objective for the next two to three years. The Strategy is now centered on Cultivating Climate & Culture.
Cultivating Climate & Culture: To create a culture that values data use and fosters continuous learn-
ing in a climate that is safe, caring, inclusive and reflective of our core values.
Over the last five years, we adhered to our Strategy action plans. Guided by those action plans and our 5-Year
Staffing Plan, we pursued and secured funding from grants to supplement our local budget in order to execute the
Strategy. As a result, the district was able to:
• Add a Director of Teaching & Learning; Title I Coordinator; Literacy, Math, and Co-Teaching Coaches
• Increase district behavioral health staffing from six (6) guidance counselors and one (1) social worker to six (6)
guidance counselors and five (5) social workers
• Adopt a standards-aligned, rigorous on-grade-level curriculum in ELA/Literacy K-8, math K-5 and pilot math
• Adopt a districtwide Tier 1 SEL curriculum
• Implement district benchmark assessments in literacy and math
• Add assessment tools to gather data in order to determine need for intervention
• Create an intervention model for academics and behavioral health
• Create a referral process for intervention
Now, with staff, curriculum and best practices in place, we are seeing improved student outcomes. We must con-
tinue to strengthen differentiation in instruction to meet the needs of all learners at all levels.
The district continues working to build a more inclusive culture in our schools. We have participated in several
recruitment fairs to promote Lunenburg Public Schools employment opportunities to a more diverse pool of appli-
cants. We have also established a Culture & Climate Council comprised of parents/guardians, staff and high school
student representatives. This Council is currently working to articulate the roles of the student, parent/guardian,
and educator in the education of each student. We believe articulating the roles and responsibilities in the relation-
ship will ultimately foster more family engagement in the education of our students.
The School Committee has also maintained a focus on the aging Turkey Hill Elementary School. The building pre-
sents challenges and limitations for our teachers in terms of delivery of instruction in the modern era to elementary
school-aged students. Our challenges include limited electrical outlets in classrooms and lack of energy efficiency,
which is particularly evident with very warm or very cold weather conditions. The building has aging systems and
system failures is a concern. It is important for the administration, School Committee, and other town boards and
committees to continue to engage in discussion regarding the future of Turkey Hill Elementary School.
Over the last five years, we have utilized all available resources and worked with intent to impact student achieve-
ment and overall well-being in the post-COVID years and beyond. We have remained true to the Strategy for Con-
tinuous Improvement. There are now materials, structures, procedures, and expectations in place; however, if we
expect to see continued improvement in student achievement, proper staffing levels are necessary. This will be one
of our greatest challenges in the next few years as the additional grant funding sources wane.

As a first-year Superintendent, I could not have asked for a better, more productive 2022-
2023 school year. While I have been a part of this extraordinary educational community
for ten years, the perspective from which I am now able to view our work, our
accomplishments, and certainly our student achievements, has shifted and given me new
purpose. I am honored and humbled to lead Montachusett Regional Vocational
Technical School District, and am proud to share a few highlights in the following report.
Workforce training continues to be a priority at the local, state and federal levels, with
additional funding meant to incentivize schools like Monty Tech to get creative, and
develop new training programs for high school students and adult learners seeking a
career change. Monty Tech School of Continuing Education has expanded outreach to
market all-new, no-cost vocational training programs to unemployed or underemployed
individuals. Having received more than $1.6M in workforce training funds from Commonwealth Corporation to
support this effort, the School of Continuing Education now offers free vocational training programs in Carpentry,
CNC Operation, Culinary Arts, Electrical, HVAC Repair, Plumbing, and Welding. These programs are designed
to provide participants with opportunities to earn valuable industry-recognized credentials, hands-on learning
experiences, and job placement services upon program completion. At press, 42 adult learners have successfully
completed their programs, been placed in jobs that align with their newfound skillset, and have been successfully
employed for more than 3 months. This is an effort we continue to be so proud of.
While we have enjoyed expanding access to our instructional spaces, training equipment, and technology to serve
our evening students, we remain committed to seeking competitive grant funding that will allow us to improve and
update instructional spaces so that our high school students stay ahead of the curve in their training and career
aspirations. With more than 230 students participating in the popular co-op program, working and learning from
experienced tradesmen and women in our area, our commitment to align our training programs to serve the needs
of our region's workforce has never been more important. In 2022-2023, we heard from a local metal fabrication
employer who asked us to consider adding a specific certitication to our curriculum, so our graduates would be
better prepared to enter the workforce without a delay or need for additional training. So without hesitation, our
instructors added the necessary lessons, and embedded an OSHA 10 Construction certification into the program.
We heard from a local restaurant owner who asked if we could expand our training to include more sous vide
preparation and improved knife skills to the students' training regimen. That request was honored immediately,
and a student is curently working with that restaurant owner, demonstrating his improved skillset. We know that
training students on new and improved equipment, while adapting and modifying our curiculum to address
immediate workforce needs will, in the end, serve our students best - our ultimate goal. Monty Tech is steadfast
in its commitment to providing a highly-skilled workforce to its industry partners throughout our region.
Finally, and perhaps the most transformative accomplishment in 2022-2023, is an innovation that does not serve
the immediate Monty Tech school community, but rather will benefit high school students enrolled in Fitchburg,
Gardner and Narragansett Regional School Districts. While we have significantly expanded and updated our
training programs, there are still so many young people without access, who would benefit from meaningfil career
and technical education. To that end, we researched, applied for, and received a $1.9M grant that will allow us to
develop an all-new vocational training space, designed to serve high school students during the day, and even more
adult learners in the evening. Dubbed the Montachusett Vocational Partnership (MVP) Academy, this new training
space will open its doors to more than 80 students in Fall 2024. We are honored to lead this trailblazing partnership,
and expect it to become a model other vocational schools will emulate in the coming years.
Thank you for your continued support of Monty Tech - a school that I am so honored to lead.

The Monty Tech Cooperative Education Program is an extension of the student's technical education that
combines classroom instruction with on-the-job-training. The popular Co-op Program provides students with
an opportunity to fither develop academic, technical and employability skills in an industry-related work
environment. All students are eligible to participate in the Co-op Program, provided they satisfy state and
school grade, attendance and performance requirements, and all Co-op students must have completed the
OSHA recognized Career Safe online health and safety course prior to being placed in a work environment..
Students Participating in the Cooperative Education Program
The Cooperative Education Program is beneficial for both student and employer. For the student, it is a chance
to gain on-the-job training that improves both their technical proficiency and employability skills, and making
industry connections enhances post-graduate employment opportunities. The Co-op Program also allows
students to earn while they learn, which has allowed many students to learn valuable life skills, financial
literacy skills, and gain a deeper understanding of the importance of career advancement and self-advocacy.
Employer benefits include addressing workforce needs in an efficient manner. Co-op students provide a pool of
trained talent, ready to assume temporary, part-time or even full-time opportunities, thus reducing employer training costs.
Co-op work hours may also be tailored to suit the needs of partnering employers.
In 2022-2023, the school saw a return to the workplace, and significant increases in the number of students
placed in this valuable training program. With approximately 100 area employers participating in Cooperative
Education, providing valuable experience to 236 students by the end of the 2022-2023 school year, school
officials remain grateful for their continued support, and look forward to future collaborations..
